questions.question: Insolation arrives at the top of the atmosphere at about 1 367 watts per square metre above every latitude. The tropics still end up hotter mainly because:
options: The sun burns hotter over the equator
A high angle of incidence lands the beam on a small footprint near the equator, while oblique rays near the poles spread the identical beam over a far larger area
Tropical air is thinner than polar air
The equator is closer to the sun's core

questions.question: Path length punishes high latitudes because:
options: Polar rays leave the sun later in the day
The poles face away from the sun at all times
A low-angle ray must slide through several times the thickness of atmosphere, so more energy is scattered, reflected and absorbed before reaching the ground
Cold air blocks all radiation

questions.question: The albedo figures used in the lesson are approximately:
options: Fresh snow and ice reflect 80 to 90 per cent; dark open ocean reflects under 10 per cent
Ocean reflects 80 to 90 per cent; snow reflects under 10 per cent
Every natural surface reflects about a third
Albedo is measured only over deserts

questions.question: The standard budget for insolation arriving at the top of the atmosphere is roughly:
options: Half reflected, half absorbed by clouds
90 per cent absorbed at the surface, 10 per cent reflected
20 per cent reflected, 30 per cent absorbed by the atmosphere, half lost to space
30 per cent reflected to space, 20 per cent absorbed in the atmosphere, about half absorbed at the surface

subtopics.title: The Axis, the Revolution and the Seasons

questions.question: Parallelism refers to:
options: The axis staying tilted at 23,5 degrees AND keeping that lean pointed in the same direction in space throughout the year
The equator lying parallel to the orbit
The tilt reversing every six months
Lines of latitude never meeting

questions.question: Around 21 June the overhead sun stands at:
options: The equator, giving equal day and night
The Tropic of Capricorn, giving our longest day
The Tropic of Cancer, 23,5 degrees north — the southern hemisphere's winter solstice and shortest day
The South Pole

questions.question: Johannesburg lies at 26 degrees south. Its midday solar altitude on 22 December, with the sun overhead at 23,5 degrees south, is:
options: 40,5 degrees
87,5 degrees, because 90 minus the angular distance of 26 minus 23,5 equals 90 minus 2,5
63,5 degrees
49,5 degrees

questions.question: The strongest single argument that distance from the sun does NOT drive the seasons is:
options: The orbit is perfectly circular
The sun's output changes with the seasons
The tilt is too small to matter
The earth is nearest the sun in early January, which is southern summer and northern winter at the same time — one distance cannot produce opposite seasons

subtopics.title: How Energy Moves Through the Atmosphere

questions.question: Warmth reaching your face across the gap when you open a hot oven door is an example of:
options: Radiation — energy travelling as electromagnetic waves without needing a medium
Advection
Latent heat
Convection

questions.question: Conduction plays almost no role above the lowest few centimetres of the atmosphere because:
options: Conduction requires darkness
Air is a very poor conductor, so molecule-to-molecule transfer happens only where air physically touches a hot surface
The upper air is too dry to conduct
Conduction works only inside metals

questions.question: The cool afternoon sea breeze arriving in East London is best classified as:
options: Convection
Radiation
Advection — heat and coolness carried horizontally by moving air
Conduction

questions.question: Latent heat moves more energy poleward than any other atmospheric process because:
options: Water vapour is heavier than air
Condensation absorbs energy from the surroundings
It operates only at the equator where energy is greatest
Evaporating each kilogram of water banks about 2,5 megajoules invisibly in the vapour, which travels vast distances before condensation pays the energy out again

subtopics.title: Surplus, Deficit and the Global Heat Engine

questions.question: The permanent energy surplus zone lies roughly:
options: Between 40 degrees north and 40 degrees south, where absorbed shortwave exceeds longwave lost to space
Poleward of 60 degrees in both hemispheres
Only along the Greenwich meridian
Between the two polar circles

questions.question: We can be certain that energy is exported poleward because:
options: The poles are slowly disappearing
The tropics would otherwise heat without limit and the poles cool without limit, yet the equator-to-pole temperature gap stays broadly stable over decades
Wind always blows toward the equator
Ocean water is warmer than air

questions.question: The division of the poleward heat freight between the two carriers is approximately:
options: All of it by ocean currents
Half by air and half by ocean
Three-quarters by the atmosphere and one-quarter by the oceans
One-tenth by the atmosphere and the rest by ocean

questions.question: South Africa's coasts display the oceanic correction because:
options: Both currents flow southward together
The two coasts share a single warm current
Neither coast has a permanent current
The warm Agulhas Current carries tropical water south past East London while the cold Benguela Current draws sub-Antarctic water north past Lambert's Bay

questions.question: Swinging the hosepipe from straight down to a low angle turns a soaked circle into a long, barely damp stripe because:
options: The same flow of water is being shared across a much larger area — the fate of sunlight arriving at high latitudes
The tap pressure drops when the nozzle tilts
Water evaporates faster at an angle
The lawn absorbs less water in the shade

questions.question: The packed school corridor stands for:
options: Albedo
Path length — slanting rays travel much further through the atmosphere and lose energy to scattering and absorption along the whole route
The greenhouse effect
Ocean currents

questions.question: The white shirts against the black tracksuit on sports day illustrate:
options: Latent heat
Convection
Albedo — pale surfaces such as snow fling sunlight back while dark surfaces such as the open ocean swallow nearly all of it
Conduction

subtopics.title: The Orange on a Leaning Needle

questions.question: The rule that the knitting needle keeps its lean and never changes the direction it points represents:
options: Parallelism — the axis holds a fixed lean in a fixed direction all year, which is what makes the overhead sun migrate
The earth spinning once a day
The moon pulling the axis upright
The orbit being elliptical

questions.question: For Johannesburg, the seasonal change in solar energy is doubled up because:
options: Cloud cover doubles in winter
The midday sun drops 47 degrees from December to June AND daylight shrinks from close to fourteen hours to about ten and a half — weaker rays for fewer hours
The city moves further from the equator in winter
Only day length changes; sun height stays the same

questions.question: At the equinoxes around 21 March and 23 September:
options: The southern hemisphere has its shortest day
The sun stands over the Tropic of Capricorn
The candle shines square on the orange's middle — the sun is overhead at the equator and day and night are equal everywhere
The earth reaches its greatest distance from the sun

questions.question: A friend claims June is cold because the earth has drifted far from the sun. The decisive reply is:
options: The earth never changes its distance from the sun
Distance matters only at the equator
June is actually the earth's closest approach
We are nearest the sun in early January, during our summer and Europe's winter — the axial lean, not distance, makes the seasons

subtopics.title: The Kitchen and the Power Grid

questions.question: The teaspoon handle that turns burning hot while standing in a mug of tea demonstrates:
options: Conduction — heat creeping along by direct molecular contact
Radiation
Advection
Latent heat

questions.question: The porridge pot turning itself over, scaled up to province size, becomes:
options: A berg wind on the coast
Convection — warm air rising over the heated interior until it builds the Free State's afternoon thunderstorms
Fog over a cold current
The greenhouse effect

questions.question: Washing drying on the line, and a damp shirt feeling cold in the wind, both show:
options: Radiation
Conduction
Latent heat — evaporation steals heat and hides it in the vapour, to be released far away when condensation occurs
Albedo

questions.question: In the power-grid picture of the planet's energy budget:
options: The poles generate the surplus and the tropics consume it
Each latitude keeps exactly the energy it receives
Transmission fails every winter
The tropics are the generating stations with a surplus, the poles run a deficit, the winds carry about three units in four and the ocean currents carry the rest
